demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette:
Kofi remembers a time, not so long ago, when the smell of turpentine was a comfort and the quiet of his studio was a sanctuary. For forty years, painting had been more than a job; it was the language he used to make sense of the world. Now, at fifty-five, he hasn't picked up a brush in eight months. The studio, a converted garage behind his house, remains locked. He can't bring himself to step inside, not since the day his wife, Amara, called him there, her voice a shattered thing on the other end of the line. That phone call was the start of the new world, the one he now inhabits. He had been sketching, planning a new canvas, when he heard her scream his name. He ran, the phone dropping from his hand, across the lawn and into the house he now feels is a trap.

He found their son, David, twenty-eight years old and impossibly vital, collapsed on the living room floor. The memory doesn't play like a film for Kofi; it exists as a series of blindingly clear photographs. He sees David's favorite grey t-shirt against the dark wood of the floor. He sees the frantic, useless pumping of his own hands on his son's chest. He sees the flashing red and blue lights painting the walls as the paramedics rushed in. These images arrive without warning, hijacking his vision while he tries to read a book or talk to Amara. Yet this terror is not the only way the memory ambushes him. Sometimes, Amara will mention a happy moment with David, or Kofi will see a photo of his son's broad smile, and he'll try to hold onto that feeling. But the effort to remember the good times inevitably brings him back to the living room floor. When that happens, the memory brings not terror, but a tidal wave of grief so profound it feels physical, a crushing weight on his chest that steals his breath and leaves him doubled over, unable to speak. At other times, something even worse happens. He will be standing in the kitchen and suddenly be engulfed by a wave of pure, suffocating panic, the full emotional force of that afternoon, but with no picture to anchor it. It's a raw, formless dread that leaves him gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape.

The world outside the house has become a minefield. The wail of a distant ambulance, once a sound he could easily ignore, now sends a jolt of ice through his veins, forcing him to brace against a wall until it passes. At a recent neighborhood gathering, a well-meaning friend began talking about losing his own father years ago. Kofi felt an immediate, overwhelming need to flee. He excused himself abruptly, leaving Amara to make apologies. He feels utterly set apart from others, as if he is behind a thick pane of glass, watching people live lives that no longer seem real or accessible. He knows they cannot understand the chasm that has opened up in his own. He has come to believe his life has been irrevocably destroyed, that the man he was-the father, the husband, the artist-died in that living room with his son.

His own home offers no refuge. Even with the doors locked and the alarm set, he feels profoundly on guard. His body is a coiled spring, his shoulders permanently hunched, his jaw clenched. Amara tells him he never relaxes, not even in his sleep. Night is the worst. The darkness seems to amplify every creak of the house, every rustle of leaves outside, and he lies awake for hours, certain that some new, unseen danger is waiting to strike. He no longer recognizes the man he sees in the mirror. The vibrant, confident artist is gone, replaced by a haunted stranger with hollow eyes. It was after a particularly bad night, followed by a morning where the sound of a passing ambulance left him trembling and nauseous, that he finally conceded to Amara's gentle pleas to seek help. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that this new, fractured self is all he will ever be.
